extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literary criticism; poets and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging poetry (here applied to Wordsworth): style, diction, imagination, imagery, emotional tone, originality, and suitability to intended readers. The page is a critical essay offering general evaluative principles illustrated with examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blameless style / untranslatableness
rubrics_metrics.description: A blameless style is tested by its 'untranslatableness' into other words of the same language without injury to the meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge proposes this as an 'infallible test' of pure style: every line and phrase may pass the ordeal of deliberate choice. He notes this is attainable (perhaps barely) in poetry, and that such a style resists affectation and misappropriation. Examples are given by praise of Wordsworth's diction; anti-patterns include promiscuous authorship and over-familiar modern phraseology that corrupts style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision of word-meaning and associative content
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaning of a word includes not only its referent but all the associations it recalls; language must convey the object and the character, mood, and intentions of the speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate diction by whether word-choice preserves both denotation and associative/cultural resonances. Coleridge argues that habituating oneself to strict accuracy of expression secures moral and intellectual benefits and helps guard against indistinct watch-words that foster fanaticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom from affectation and misappropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction should be uncorrupted by affectations or misappropriations produced by promiscuous authorship or disproportionate exposure to contemporary fashions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial self-possession and fine distinction protect against the 'infection' of tasteless or perverted phrases common in sermons, newspapers, legislative harangues, and convivial speeches. Anti-pattern: allowing quotidian corrupt eloquence to pervade one’s prose or verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight and sanity of thoughts and sentiments (authenticity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thoughts and sentiments should have correspondent weight and sanity, won from the poet's own meditative observation rather than merely from books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge values 'fresh' sentiments 'with the dew upon them' — original insights grounded in contemplation. He contrasts genuine meditative origin with bookish or borrowed sentiment; examples from Wordsworth’s poems are cited to illustrate such authentic reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and meditative observation (source of ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetical material should arise from the poet’s own meditative observation instead of being second-hand from other authors or fashions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether reflections feel 'native' to the poet (not 'learnt') and whether they bear the mark of inward observation. Coleridge emphasizes that such originality makes poems valuable even when not universally popular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sinewy strength and felicity of single lines/paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent 'sinewy' strength and originality in individual lines and paragraphs; a 'curiosa felicitas' of diction—occasional striking felicities even in single lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess poems by their capacity to produce memorable, forceful lines and felicitous turns of phrase. Coleridge notes this as a distinct excellence that even critics hostile to Wordsworth conceded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth of nature in imagery and description
rubrics_metrics.description: Images and descriptions should display 'perfect truth of nature' — taken immediately from nature and showing intimacy with the spirit that gives physiognomic expression to natural objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good nature-description distinguishes detail with softness and lustre (like a reflection in a calm lake) rather than distorting. Coleridge cites skating, the green linnet, blue-cap, cuckoo, and other passages as exemplary precise yet lovely depictions drawn from direct observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meditative pathos and humane sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: A union of deep, subtle thought with sensibility: pathos that sympathizes with 'man as man' from a contemplative stance, seeing the divine or common humanity beneath differences of rank or fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the poet’s capacity to evoke genuine feeling without mere sentimentality; Coleridge points to compositions (e.g., 'The Affliction of Margaret') that move parents to tears as evidence. The pathos is philosophic and contemplative rather than purely fellow-suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative power (the highest sense of Imagination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession of Imagination in the highest and strictest sense: the creative power that 'adds the gleam' and consecration—the imaginative faculty that transforms perception into poetic vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imaginative power should be original and characteristic, comparing (in degree) to Shakespeare and Milton while remaining wholly individual. Coleridge distinguishes Imagination from mere fancy, and cites passages (Yew Trees, Resolution and Independence, the Ode) illustrating this faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspicuity for intended audience (fit audience)
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem need only be perspicuous to those for whom it is written; lack of popular understanding does not imply obscurity in a faultful sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge argues that works can be 'arduous and high' and intended for readers accustomed to introspection; criterion: clarity to the poem's fit audience rather than universal intelligibility. He quotes Dante’s lines on arduous lyric addressed to a select readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of vulgarity mistaken for simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: True simplicity must be distinguished from vulgarity or shallow popular manner; do not praise simplicity when it is actually a gilded vulgarity or affected admirers mistake vulgarity for sweetness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware the anti-pattern where admirers label a poet 'sweet, simple' when the work is in fact vulgarized or adapted for children’s play; Coleridge defends Wordsworth against charges of vulgarity and criticizes over-simplified praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational cultivation of diction and judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Early habituation to investigate meanings and choices of words cultivates judgment and verbal precision, which in turn fosters veracity and guards against fanaticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge recommends teaching youth to probe word-choice and logic, arguing that such training makes judgment a 'second nature' and improves prose and poetic style over time. This is a procedural standard linking pedagogy to literary quality.
